answers_by_date.basis: Labour Code (DFL 1/1994), art. 2, inciso 2, as it stood before July 2001. I rebuilt it from Ley 19.739, which inserted 'edad, estado civil,' between 'sexo' and 'sindicación' in that inciso. It declared discrimination on grounds including race and nationality contrary to labour-law principles. Constitution art. 19 No. 16 (free choice of work 'con una justa retribución'; ban on any discrimination not based on personal capacity) also applied. Practice evidence is thin: the US State Department 1999 report only covers minimum-wage setting, with nothing on migrants.

Ley 19.759 (in force 1 Dec 2001) rewrote art. 2. It defines 'actos de discriminación' as distinctions based on 'raza, color, ... nacionalidad, ascendencia nacional u origen social' that impair 'igualdad de oportunidades o de trato en el empleo'. DFL 1/2002 (published 16 Jan 2003) carried it into the new consolidated code. US State Department 2004 report: the Labour Code bans nationality discrimination 'however, such discrimination occurred in practice'. There is no migrant-specific wage data.

Same Labour Code art. 2. The constitutional clause was unchanged in substance after the Ley 20.050 reform (2005). Practice: the US State Department 2009 report says the government enforced the anti-discrimination bans but discrimination continued. The CMW (2011) reported exploitation and abusive conditions of women migrant domestic workers, especially irregular ones, and urged more labour inspection.

Same Labour Code art. 2. Ley 20.609 (2012) adds a general civil remedy against arbitrary discrimination based on nationality and race. Practice: the US State Department 2014 report says employment discrimination 'continued to occur'. CESCR (June 2015) found persistent discrimination against migrants 'particularly in the areas of employment'.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

answers.starting_answer_concern: The protection answer holds. Ley 21.325 arts. 13-14 were not in force on 1 Jan 2020; the 2020 answer rests on Labour Code art. 2 and Constitution art. 19 No. 16 (the citation's 'art. 16' should read art. 19 No. 16). The implementation rating 'Sometimes; Effectively Always' is not a valid neighbouring pair. I used its centre, 'Usually', for the past dates, and the documented pattern of discrimination and exploitation of migrant domestic workers fits 'Usually'.
answers.notes: No court ruling relied on. Ley 20.348 (2009, art. 62 bis) concerns only gender pay equality and was not used. The Labour Code applies to all workers regardless of nationality.

answers_by_date.answer: Employment is tied to specific employer; change of employer possible, but requires new work permit application
answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 arts. 23-25: the contract-bound visa ('residente sujeto a contrato') is granted to fulfil a specific contract, and ending that contract voids the visa, 'sin perjuicio del derecho de su titular de solicitar una nueva visación'. DS 597 art. 40 (1984 text) requires the new contract and the finiquito with the old employer for a new visa. No practice evidence specific to this period was found.

The rule is otherwise unchanged. No period-specific practice evidence was found.

answers.starting_answer_concern: Ley 21.325 arts. 70/73 and Decree 177 were not in force in 2020; the answer rests on DL 1.094 arts. 23-25 and DS 597 arts. 39-40. This fits contract-visa holders only. Temporary-visa holders (DS 597 art. 49: 'podrán desarrollar cualesquiera clase de actividad lícita') and permanent residents could choose employment freely. The rating also ignores the Labour Code art. 19 quota. The implementation rating has no documented basis in any period.
answers.notes: Executive measures of the 2010s (Mercosur residence visas from 2009, the 'motivos laborales' temporary visa of 2015, the 2018 visas) widened access to employer-independent permits. I did not read them in this session, so they are not recorded as events.

answers_by_date.basis: DS 597 art. 35 (1984 text): contract-visa dependants (spouse etc.) 'no están habilitados para realizar actividades remuneradas en el país'. Art. 49: temporary-visa dependants 'no podrán realizar actividades remuneradas'. Art. 46: the same bar applies to student dependants. A spouse needed their own visa or authorisation.
Arts. 35, 46 and 49 of DS 597 were unchanged by Decreto 2910 (2000). DL 1.094 art. 23 inciso 3 grants the same visa to family members without a work entitlement.
No change to DS 597 arts. 35/49 or DL 1.094 arts. 23/29 (Ley 20.430 of 2010 did not touch them).
Decreto 1930 (Mar 2015) amended only art. 41; arts. 35 and 49 are identical in the 2020 version.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, migrants have a right to the same employment conditions and protections
answers_by_date.basis: The Labour Code (DFL 1/1994) applies to all workers without nationality distinction: hours, rest, holidays, safety and dismissal. Art. 2 inciso 2 barred nationality-based discrimination (rebuilt from Ley 19.739). DS 597 art. 36 f) requires contract-visa contracts to comply with labour and social-security rules. The quota in arts. 19-20 limits hiring, not conditions. No migrant-specific practice evidence was found; I kept the starting level.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, migrants have a right to the same employment conditions and protections
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 19.759 (Dec 2001) defined discrimination as covering 'igualdad de oportunidades o de trato en el empleo' on nationality grounds. DFL 1/2002 kept it. US State Department 2004: such discrimination 'occurred in practice'. Evidence is thin, so I kept the starting level and flagged it.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, migrants have a right to the same employment conditions and protections

answers_by_date.basis: Same law, plus Ley 20.609 (2012). US State Department 2014: inspectors do not cover the informal economy and employment discrimination continued. CESCR 2015: persistent discrimination against migrants in employment. Starting level kept; concern noted.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The protection answer holds; Ley 21.325 art. 14 was not in force in 2020, so the 2020 answer rests on the Labour Code. The 'Effectively Always' rating looks too high. CMW 2011 and CESCR 2015 document breaches (abusive conditions of migrant domestic workers, discrimination in employment), and the US State Department notes no inspection of the informal economy. answers_by_date.basis: Labour Code (DFL 1/1994) art. 2 inciso 2 listed race among banned grounds (rebuilt from Ley 19.739). Constitution art. 19 No. 2 (no privileged groups, no arbitrary differences) and No. 16 (ban on discrimination not based on capacity) also applied. US State Department 1999 notes the Constitution 'does not ban specifically discrimination based on race'. The Labour Code ban covers employment only. Practice evidence for 2000 is minimal.

Ley 19.759 (Dec 2001) defines discrimination as distinctions based on 'raza, color, ... nacionalidad, ascendencia nacional'. US State Department 2004: the Labour Code prohibits race and nationality discrimination 'however, such discrimination occurred in practice'.

Same provisions. US State Department 2009: the government enforced the bans but discrimination continued, with skinhead violence against immigrants. The CMW (2011) noted discriminatory attitudes and stigmatisation of migrant workers.

Ley 20.609 (in force 24 Jul 2012) explicitly bans arbitrary discrimination based on 'raza o etnia, la nacionalidad' in all fields, with a judicial action. CERD (2013): migrants 'particularly those of Latin American origin, continue to face discrimination'. CESCR 2015 found the same.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

answers.starting_answer_concern: The 2020 'Yes' holds, but it rests on Ley 20.609 art. 2, Labour Code art. 2 and Constitution art. 19 No. 2, not Ley 21.325, which was not in force. Before July 2012 the express race ban was confined to employment (Labour Code art. 2). The Constitution gave only general equality, so the 2000-2010 'Yes' is narrower in scope but still a statutory race ban.
